title: Artificial intelligence in hepatitis: Advances in diagnosis, treatment optimization, and prognostic prediction.
source: PubMed · The Journal of international medical research
desc: [The Journal of international medical research] Hepatitis remains a major global health challenge and an important contributor to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality worldwide. Early diagnosis, effective treatment selection, and accurate prognostic stratification remain critical unmet needs in clinical hepatology. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a promising approach to addressing these challenges through the integration and analysis of large-scale, heterogeneous biomedical datasets. This narrative review synthesizes advances in artificial intelligence applications in hepatitis research and clinical practice published over the past decade, organized across three clinical domains: diagnosis, treatment optimization, and prognosis prediction. In the diagnostic domain, artificial intelligence-based approaches have been applied to medical imaging, digital pathology, and multi-omics data to enhance the detection, classification, and staging of liver disease. In the therapeutic domain, machine learning models have been increasingly deployed to support drug discovery, optimize therapeutic regimens, and predict individual treatment responses. In the prognostic domain, artificial intelligence-driven models have shown promising performance in predicting disease progression, survival outcomes, and clinical complications. Nevertheless, key limitations persist, including data heterogeneity, limited external generalizability, and barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will depend on prospective multicenter evaluation, use of interoperable multimodal data, development of transparent models that account for uncertainty, and evidence that artificial intelligence improves clinical decisions and patient outcomes rather than performance metrics alone.

title: Predicting the Optimal Empirical Antibiotic Therapy for Bacteremia Using an Artificial Intelligence-based Model
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Nantes University Hospital; conditions: Bacteremia; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 8765; status: COMPLETED] Bacteremia, a common infection associated with high morbidity and mortality, requires prompt and appropriate antibiotic treatment. Numerous studies have shown that the appropriate use of antibiotics helps improve the prognosis of patients, reduce the selection of pathogenic organisms, the emergence of antibiotic resistance, adverse treatment effects, and healthcare costs. The Nantes University Hospital Center has operated a Biomedical Data Warehouse (BDW) since 2018. The growing availability of data through BDWs thus enables the development of decision-support tools based on machine learning. The primary objective of the OPTIBact project is to predict the optimal empirical antibiotic for hospitalized patients with bacteremia using a machine learning-based predictive model using data from the Nantes University Hospital's BDW. As secondary objectives, the study aims: * To compare the performance of the predictive model for the optimal empirical antibiotic against standard patient care * To estimate the expected benefit of the predictive model compared to real-world practice in terms of clinical outcomes * To predict the optimal dosage of empirical antibiotic therapy * To compare the performance of the predictive model for optimal empirical antibiotic therapy dosing with standard patient care * To describe inpatient patients in Nantes University Hospital who received optimal antibiotic therapy and those who did not * To Identify predictors of antibiotic resistance in bacteria isolated from blood cultures, stratified by pathogen type.

title: ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?
desc: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Using Medical Imaging
desc: Deep learning shows promise for breast cancer diagnosis, but limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption. We benchmark ten ImageNet-pretrained models (ResNet50, VGG19, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, Xception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt, ViT, and Swin Transformer) for benign-versus-malignant classification on the BreakHis histopathology dataset using a patient-level split, and explain their predictions with Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and LRP. DenseNet121 performed best, with 99.4% test accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.999, and significantly outperformed all other models (p < 0.001). Transformer-based models trailed the CNNs. The explanations consistently highlighted nuclei-rich and glandular regions of diagnostic relevance. Combining transfer learning with explainable AI can thus yield accurate, interpretable tools for breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
desc: Multimodal deep learning models for cancer survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.

title: Xenograft supervision and joint methylation-fragment-end encoding define a reusable molecular scoring layer for cell-free tumor DNA
desc: Circulating tumor DNA is often scarce in plasma, and regional methylation summaries can obscure informative differences between individual molecules. Here we present ctDNA-BERT, a Transformer that scores individual bisulfite reads without predefined differentially methylated regions by jointly encoding CpG methylation state, nucleotide context and the fragment 3' end. Xenografts provide molecule-level tumor supervision. The resulting frozen scorer supported tumor-fraction estimation in synthetic and patient-derived xenograft mixtures and enriched tumor-concordant methylation and chromatin-accessibility signals in independent hepatocellular carcinoma and stage III pan-cancer plasma without cohort-specific retraining. Features derived from selected reads discriminated stage I cancers from healthy controls in a retrospective cohort of 1,477 specimens, achieving an out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.884. By separating molecular scoring from sample-level inference, ctDNA-BERT provides a reusable read-level scoring layer for cell-free DNA methylation analysis.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery-A Narrative Review.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly growing in the field of dental medicine and in oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS). The aim of the present review is to assess current applications of AI in OMS, to evaluate their advantages and limitations, and to identify areas requiring further research. Materials and Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with targeted keywords including "artificial intelligence," "deep learning," "machine learning," "oral surgery," "maxillofacial surgery," and "diagnosis "Artificial Intelligence" OR "Machine Learning" OR "Deep Learning" AND "Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery" OR "Oral Surgery" OR "Maxillofacial Surgery" AND "Diagnosis". Of 308 identified studies, 37 met the inclusion criteria focusing on AI-assisted detection interpretation and surgical planning in OMS. Results: AI is effective in identifying anatomical landmarks, evaluating lesions and cysts, diagnosing bone disease like medication-related osteonecrosis of jaws (MRONJ), planning dental implants, and aiding in the classification of fractures and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders. AI can match or outperform human experts in various diagnostic tasks, particularly in panoramic and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) image analysis. AI shows promise in early detection of impacted and supernumerary teeth, maxillofacial pathologies, neoplastic conditions, and soft tissue calcifications. Limitations: However, substantial methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting of AI performance metrics, and limited external validation across the included studies constrain direct comparison of results and assessment of the generalizability of reported AI performance. Conclusions: AI may assist clinicians in diagnostic and treatment-related decision-making, but current evidence does not support its use as a replacement for comprehensive clinical assessment and professional judgment.

title: AI-Simplified Discharge Summaries to Improve Patient Comprehension (ContextCare)
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Scarborough Health Network; conditions: Patient Discharge, Health Literacy; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 52; status: RECRUITING] This randomized pilot study will compare standard hospital discharge communication with discharge summaries simplified using ContextCare, an artificial intelligence-assisted application. The study will enroll 50 adults discharged from Scarborough Health Network. Participants will be assigned to one of two groups in a 1:1 ratio, with allocation stratified by baseline health literacy. The main measure is how well participants explain their diagnosis, treatment, follow-up care, and instructions for seeking further help immediately after receiving discharge information. The study will also assess satisfaction, recall after discharge, and selected post-discharge outcomes.

title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
desc: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
desc: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.

title: Building virtual cell dynamics that evolve with biological measurements
desc: Virtual cell models built from single-cell measurements need to predict how cells change over time, but new biological measurements often reveal dynamical relationships that existing models cannot express. Translating such measurements into dynamics therefore requires deciding what biological relation should be modeled, where it should enter the formulation and how its recovery should be validated. Here we present CellCompass, an agentic AI system that couples a scientific agent with an extensible dynamical engine for modeling state transitions and population change, along with fate and molecular readout. CellCompass reuses existing formulations when sufficient and designs, implements and refines new ones when experimental measurements introduce additional constraints. To assess this capability, we developed DynBench100, a benchmark of 100 simulated single-cell time-course scenarios with hidden dynamical ground truth. CellCompass achieved the highest aggregate performance among the tested general-purpose and biomedical agents across six dynamical tasks. Across four real single-cell studies, it retained an existing velocity-growth model to reconstruct context-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition and developed three new dynamical formulations for distinct experimental measurements. In drug-response data, incorporating metabolic RNA labeling reduced pulse-control identifiability error by 31.1%, revealing staged response programs and generating testable predictions for perturbing a candidate adaptive program. In hematopoietic lineage tracing, incorporating clonal barcodes improved clone-fate agreement by 54% over the strongest dynamical baseline, identifying early lineage priming among transcriptionally similar progenitors. Finally, in time-resolved CITE-seq data, CellCompass reduced future surface-protein distribution error by 13.2% for RNA-initialized trajectories, uncovering lineage-specific temporal offsets between transcriptional and protein programs. Together, CellCompass provides a framework in which virtual-cell dynamics can expand with the biological measurements used to constrain them.

title: Provider Experiences with AI Clinical Decision Support in eSanjeevani
desc: BackgroundClinical decision support systems (CDSS) are increasingly embedded in national telemedicine services, however how different stakeholders who use them experience these tools, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, is less explored. In the assisted model of Indias eSanjeevani service, spoke health workers enter structured symptoms and hub clinicians review a symptom summary and an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated differential diagnosis. ObjectiveTo describe role-specific experiences of eSanjeevanis CDSS functions and to estimate how acceptance coexists with specific reported difficulties within each role. MethodsWe analyzed a program feedback web survey completed between 11 July and 29 July, 2025 by hub clinicians and spoke providers. Prespecified item profiles covered review of summaries and suggested diagnoses, the perceived relation of suggestions to the clinicians own diagnosis, ease of use and intention to use (hub), and symptom-capture utility, question quantity, question relevance, summary presentation and satisfaction (spoke). Within-role contrasts were reported as absolute differences in acceptance with Newcombe 95% CIs. Short open comments underwent content analysis. ResultsThe cohort comprised 190 hub and 662 spoke respondents from 13 and 15 states (21.4% and 19.3% of eligible providers). Among hub respondents, 76.8% regularly reviewed the symptom summary and 58.9% the suggested diagnoses; 72.6% judged suggestions matched (32.6%) or appropriate but different (40.0%), 7.9% mostly inappropriate, and 11.1% reported that suggestions were mostly not generated. Overall, 85.3% intended to keep using the tools. Affirmative intention was 98.4% when suggestions matched, 66.7% when they were mostly inappropriate (difference vs matched or appropriate-23.2 percentage points, 95% CI-48.5 to-4.0) and 61.9% when mostly absent (-25.7, 95% CI-47.1 to-7.3); technical issues, reported by 38.4%, made little difference (-2.8, 95% CI-14.1 to 7.3). Among spoke respondents, 63.4% rated question quantity appropriate, with miscalibration in both directions (15.6% too many; 16.6% too few); 89.9% found the questions relevant and 91.8% found the summary clear. Satisfaction was 75.3% and did not differ materially between those reporting too many questions and those reporting an appropriate number (-2.7, 95% CI-12.8 to 6.0). title: Cardiac Computed Tomography in Infective Endocarditis: A Radiological Perspective on Structural Complications and Emerging Diagnostic Technologies.
desc: [Tomography (Ann Arbor, Mich.)] Background: Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a life-threatening disease associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography are the first-line imaging modalities, but their diagnostic performance may be reduced in patients with prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices, previous cardiac surgery, extensive calcification, or suspected periannular extension. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) provides complementary high-resolution anatomical information and has gained increasing importance within contemporary multimodality diagnostic pathways. Scope: This Review critically examines the current role of cardiac CT in IE, including acquisition and reconstruction strategies, lesion-specific imaging findings, applications in native, prosthetic, transcatheter, and device-related infection, extracardiac assessment, and preoperative planning. Comparative observations regarding echocardiography and selected multimodality techniques are integrated where directly relevant. Emerging applications of spectral CT, photon-counting detector CT, deep learning reconstruction, radiomics, and artificial intelligence are appraised according to four levels of evidence: clinically validated IE applications, preliminary IE-specific evidence, indirect cardiovascular evidence, and conceptual applications. Main Findings: Cardiac CT is particularly valuable for detecting and anatomically characterizing periannular complications, including abscesses, pseudoaneurysms, fistulous tracts, inflammatory extension, and prosthetic dehiscence. Multiphase electrocardiography (ECG)-gated acquisition improves the assessment of dynamic valvular and prosthetic abnormalities. Transesophageal echocardiography remains more sensitive for small or highly mobile vegetations, leaflet perforation, regurgitant jets, and intracardiac flow abnormalities, demonstrating that the two techniques are complementary rather than interchangeable. Cardiac CT also contributes to coronary assessment, surgical planning, evaluation of previous grafts and reconstructive material, and selected extracardiac complications. Conclusions: Cardiac CT is an important component of contemporary multimodality IE assessment, but it should not be regarded as a replacement for echocardiography. Its clinical value depends on the infected substrate, suspected complication, acquisition protocol, and integration with echocardiographic, microbiological, surgical, and clinical findings. title: What Should we Measure? A Qualitative Interview Study on Outcomes for Evaluating AI-assisted Medical Image Interpretation.
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Oxford; conditions: Artificial Intelligence Perception and Attitude; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 30; status: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Background: AI (artificial intelligence) tools are increasingly used to help clinicians interpret medical images such as X-rays, scans, skin photographs and eye images. In most cases the AI does not work alone: a clinician makes the final decision, using the AI as support. Before these tools are used in the NHS, they must be tested to show they are safe and helpful. They are usually tested in a "reader study", where several clinicians each interpret the same set of images, sometimes with the AI's help and sometimes without, so performance can be compared. These studies tend to focus on whether the diagnosis was correct. However, accuracy alone may not measure everything that matters. For example, what happens when the AI gets it wrong, whether clinicians rely on it too much or too little, or how the tool affects efficiency. At present there is no agreed standard for what these studies should measure, so important things are often missed and studies are hard to compare. Aim: The aim of this study is to find out, by talking to people with different perspectives, which outcomes are important when evaluating AI tools that help clinicians read medical images. Objectives: 1. Explore which outcomes people think matter when judging whether an AI tools is safe and good enough to use 2. Understand the reasons behind their views 3. Explore how priorities differ between groups, such as patients and developers. The output will be a list of important candidate outcomes, which will feed into a future project to agree a recommended set of outcomes for these studies (a "core outcome set"). Research value: Without agreement on what to measure, studies of AI tools may overlook outcomes that matter, and their results are difficult to compare and combine. Hearing directly from the people affected, rather than relying only on what previous studies happened to measure, helps ensure the recommended set reflects people's priorities. This will lead to better-designed studies and AI tools that are safer and more useful in practice. Outline of the research: The investigators will interview 24-30 people who have a stake in how these tools are tested and used, including clinicians, researchers, developers, people involved in regulation, and patients and members of the public. Interviews will last 45-60 minutes and will take place using Microsoft Teams. title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
desc: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.
